visible.summary:
In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an 'abominable' one defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across Nigeria in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.

Edo's finding is the Ekpoma killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal 'community justice' invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.
visible.tangentialFactors: The documented lethal incidents here concern male same-sex conduct rather than gender expression directly; their weight for trans visitors is the demonstrated capacity for community-justice killing with impunity in a customary-authority setting.

sources.claim: Nigerian Observer (May 2018): in Ekpoma a mob lynched one of two men caught together and the other escaped, framed as an 'abominable act' under traditional heritage. Documents fatal community violence in Edo State.

The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIERs) '2024 Human Rights Violations Report' (published January 2025): annual documentation of violations based on real or perceived SOGIESC in Nigeria; per the dossier, its 2024 edition records 556 violations affecting 850 victims across the reporting period and states these represent only a fraction of the true scale.

On 10 June 2010 The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City (Oredo LGA, Edo State) that a middle-aged man, Mark Osato Edomwonyi, narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment; a neighbour raised the alarm and Mark fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, which then 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution is recorded in the report, and Mark's whereabouts were still unknown at filing. First incident-level evidence for Edo beyond the 2018 Ekpoma killing: lethal mob 'community justice' operates in the state capital too, with no documented law-enforcement response.

The Nigerian Observer reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were caught in the act in a remote community in Edo State in February 2008; a mob mercilessly beat the two for desecrating the community, Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived, and the police arrested Jerry for interrogation. Direct evidence that Edo's police machinery pursued same-sex couples on the ground in 2008 — a community lynching attempt answered by arrest and a wanted declaration rather than protection.

visible.summary:
North West sits squarely in the former-Bantustan geography where the traditional-courts jurisdiction is most extensive following the Bantustan-era map: HRW's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies these areas as a "separate legal system" whose adjudication of gender and sexual matters under customary law with a consent presumption against the individual constitutes the principal sub-national legal divergence in South Africa. The Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended; the replacement Bill (TKLB) has been delayed. No province has religious criminal law; no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

North West is also the only province outside Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study (2010; the GALA-hosted Love Not Hate review records only three quantitative studies ever attempted nationally), giving it a data-presence signal: incidents against queer people here are, historically, more likely to appear in research rather than only in the "dark figure" of unreported crime that characterises most provinces. No trans-specific incident series was found. The 2010 study covers gay and lesbian people; its relevance to a trans visitor is as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy province.

The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. Limpopo (0.65), the two share the former-Bantustan customary-authority finding at similar magnitude; North West's additional 2010 data presence does not raise it above Limpopo because the study documents violence prevalence rather than institutional response capacity. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), North West sits higher because KZN adds a retrieved township queerphobia study and the Zulu king / CONTRALESA official alignment against queer people; North West has the jurisdictional risk without a comparable named-authority statement. vs. Western Cape (0.72) and Gauteng (0.71), the gap reflects metro institutional functioning versus rural customary-authority geography. The dossier's under-reporting caveat applies equally: a province with more recorded hate crime may simply have better reporting than more danger.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2010 provincial prevalence study documents hate crime against gay and lesbian people; for a trans visitor it works as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy province.

sources.claim: HRW (29 May 2012): the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans; HRW reports rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas, and the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016): the companion review of hate crimes against LGBT people in South Africa states that only three quantitative studies have ever been done - the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape; a 2010 North West province study; and this national campaign study - and measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

The trans community in North West province cannot access hormone replacement therapy (HRT) at any public health facility in the province and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to get it, MambaOnline reported on 21 February 2023. The North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people, in its response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the SA Human Rights Commission. Documents the province-level absence of trans-specific healthcare that a trans visitor reliant on prescribed HRT would confront on the ground.

MambaOnline (23 March 2016, citing the Taung Daily News) reported that 18-year-old lesbian Zinzi Manini Molema of Maphoitsile village, North West, was barred from attending school for refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home saying she must wear a skirt 'since I was a girl', and she stayed home for three weeks without attending any classes. Records a North West institution enforcing a gendered dress code against a gender-nonconforming pupil, illustrating the province's socially conservative enforcement climate.

A report entitled 'Same-sex sexuality in North-West province', released in October 2010, presented the results of a survey conducted under the auspices of the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology during 2009 and 2010, with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella collaborating; it surveyed 319 LGBT people from a largely rural background in one of the country's poorest and most under-populated provinces, asking about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT persons perceive their environment, and sexual abuse and discrimination. Provides the province-level 2010 survey behind this record's data-presence signal for North West.

visible.summary:
Chechnya's security apparatus operates outside legal constraint on this question. In February 2017, law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge: dozens of men were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities, starved and tortured; some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families 'barely alive from beatings' after their captors exposed them to relatives encouraged to carry out honour killings (Human Rights Watch, 2017). Independent domestic reporting in January 2019 found the persecution resuming and the documented secret facility active again, while the regional leader's press office denied such sites exist. Since 2022, two investigations have documented detained homosexual men blackmailed into 'volunteering' for front-line conscription in Russia's war in Ukraine (at least seven sent, one killed) and a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced mobilisation. The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records systematic campaigns in this republic and the wider North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024 — abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings — and assesses trans people and visible advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with such violence spreading beyond the region after the 2023 'extremist movement' designation.

For a discovered or outed visitor: detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy.
visible.tangentialFactors: The documented campaigns - the 2017 purge, the conscription blackmail - targeted men perceived as homosexual; trans-specific detentions in the republic are not separately tabulated in these sources, but the same unofficial-detention apparatus is what an official immigration assessment treats as likely to persecute trans people in the region.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Frequent terrorist attacks and general armed instability in the republic, cited by Western travel advisories for all visitors, are separate from trans-specific risk.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (26 May 2017): documents the Feb 2017 Chechen police purge — men believed gay rounded up, held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured; some forcibly disappeared, others returned to families 'barely alive from beatings', captors outing them and urging honour killings. Report shows Kadyrov's denial notwithstanding that top regional officials knew. The core sourced basis for this record's extreme-risk profile.

Novaya Gazeta (11 Jan 2019, Russian): learned of renewed persecution of gay men in Chechnya — warnings circulated via VKontakte LGBT-group admins telling those still at large to leave the republic; Kadyrov press secretary Alvi Karimov denied the reports. Follows the paper's April 2017 investigation into torture and killings of gay men for which no criminal case was opened. Establishes the purge reactivated within two years, not a one-off.

The Insider (4 Sep 2024): SK SOS reports Chechen security forces coercing detained gay men into military service — at least seven sent to frontlines in Ukraine, one already killed; methods began before the 21 Sep 2022 mobilisation order. In early Sep 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned they'd be sent to front. Establishes detention-to-frontline blackmail as an ongoing persecution vector since 2022.

OC Media (Memorial Human Rights Centre investigation): a mass wave of unlawful detentions sweeping Chechnya with detainees forcibly sent to fight in Ukraine — people detained over minor pretexts (missing insurance documents), taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, forced to sign contracts; families sometimes must recruit two 'volunteers' to free a detained relative. Complements the gay-specific coercion reports: conscription machinery as a generalised coercive tool of the Chechen security apparatus.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across this republic and the wider North Caucasus 2017–2024 (abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings); assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; notes the 2023 'extremist organisation' designation of the international LGBT+ movement exposing support/activity to 2–6 years (organising 6–10) imprisonment, with violence spreading beyond the region. The freshest official-assessment source for the record's trans-specific claim.

visible.summary:
The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) identifies the North Caucasus — including Dagestan — as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, documenting systematic campaigns by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS's director states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that the situation worsens year on year.

Canada's travel advisory tells travellers to avoid all travel to Russia, names Dagestan among the republics where terrorist attacks are frequent, and warns that special permission from the Ministry of the Interior is required to enter certain areas — an access regime that also hampers independent monitoring of how state and customary authority operate on the ground.

For a visitor the risk here is the regional pattern: the federal ‘extremist’ designation of 2023, which extended violence in detention beyond the region, combined with local security structures and family-honour norms that produce extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process. No separate Dagestan-specific written law targeting trans people exists, and no Chechnya-scale documented purge infrastructure is attributed to this republic.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 'no safe life' assessment and the shared security-and-custom enforcement logic concern LGBTIQ+ people broadly rather than tabulating trans-specific cases in the republic.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Advisories cite frequent terrorist attacks and instability across the North Caucasus for all travellers; that general insecurity is distinct from the trans-specific exception the same advisories carve out.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): names the North Caucasus — including Dagestan — as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities 2017–2024 (abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings); assesses trans people and visible advocates specifically. Freshest official assessment anchoring this record's regional-pattern claim.

Global Affairs Canada Russia advisory (retrieved for this review): advises avoid all travel; flags frequent terrorist attacks in the republics of Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai; states special permission from the Ministry of the Interior is required to enter certain areas and regions; and warns violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons occurs, particularly in the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan. The record's access-regime claim (MOI permission hampering monitoring) comes from here.

Human Rights House Foundation interview with David Isteev (North Caucasus SOS, working in exile): 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families'; situation worsens year on year. Testimony-based regional assessment underpinning this record's 'no safe private existence' line.

visible.summary:
The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus as the exception to its general finding on Russia: people in the region, trans people, and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities from 2017 to 2024 included abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, where even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families.

Canada's advisory against all travel to Russia names Ingushetia among the republics where terrorist attacks are frequent and warns that entering certain areas requires special permission from the Ministry of the Interior; the special-access regime also limits independent monitoring. Like neighbouring Dagestan, Ingushetia has no documented republic-specific purge infrastructure on the scale recorded for Chechnya.

The risk for a discovered visitor is federal hostility operating through local security structures and family-honour norms — extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process — rather than any Ingushetia-specific written provision against trans people.
visible.tangentialFactors: The named-permission regime and the 'no safe life' finding apply to the republic as part of an LGBTIQ+ group broadly; no republic-specific trans purge infrastructure is documented.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Frequent terrorist attacks, cited for all travellers to this republic, are a general-security factor distinct from trans risk.

sources.claim: Global Affairs Canada Russia advisory (retrieved for this review): advises avoid all travel; lists Ingushetia among republics with frequent terrorist attacks (with Chechnya, Dagestan, Stavropol Krai); notes foreigner surveillance and specifically that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, allies and families have been attacked, harassed and abused; since Jan 2024 organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as 'extremist'; MOI special permission required to enter certain areas. Named-in-source access/security facts for this record.

Human Rights House Foundation interview with David Isteev (North Caucasus SOS): 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families'; annual deterioration attested by an on-the-ground defender working in exile. Regional testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): treats the North Caucasus (incl. this republic) as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory Russia finding — trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; documents systematic regional campaigns 2017–2024; 2023 'extremist' designation exposes LGBT+ activity to 2–6 (organising 6–10) years' imprisonment, violence spreading beyond the region.

visible.summary:
The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus as the exception within Russia: people in the region, trans people, and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, amid documented systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people from 2017 to 2024 that included abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS — which coordinates roughly 34 evacuations a year of people fleeing the region — states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, where even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families.

No Karachay-Cherkessia-specific purge infrastructure is documented. The visitor-facing risk is therefore the regional pattern rather than any locally recorded apparatus: the 2023 federal ‘extremist’ designation, after which violence in detention spread beyond the region, operating through security practices and family-honour norms that can produce extrajudicial outcomes unmediated by legal process.
visible.tangentialFactors: The informal-enforcement pattern documented for the zone - round-ups, detention, family exposure, violence unmediated by legal process - was first recorded against gay men and LGBTIQ+ people generally rather than trans people specifically; the same security-and-custom logic operates on any discovered queer visitor, trans or not.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The Western don't-travel designation for the North Caucasus zone is driven largely by general armed-conflict and security risk that affects all travellers; the trans-relevant content is the LGBT-specific exception drawn by the UK Home Office note, not the blanket advisory level.

sources.claim: Human Rights House Foundation interview with David Isteev (North Caucasus SOS): 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families'; year-on-year deterioration from an on-the-ground defender in exile. Regional testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): singles out the North Caucasus (incl. this republic) as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory Russia finding — trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; systematic regional campaigns 2017–2024; 2023 'extremist' designation → 2–6 (organising 6–10) years' imprisonment.
